text: 🇲🇽🏭 "In 28 years of exports, there has never been a case of screwworm in Michoacán." — Columba López, Secretary of Agriculture, Plan Michoacán report, Nov 4, 2026 After a price collapse disrupted the avocado harvest for three weeks, packers and workers reached a deal late Tuesday night, and exports resume. The Agriculture Secretary said viral screwworm videos were misrepresented: one load in Jalisco was headed to an oil plant, not export, and in Nayarit the larvae were in the boxes, not the fruit. Every orchard is registered, and 500 hectares are inspected at random each month. Sheinbaum said avocados from other countries now compete with Mexico's. Exporters will soon need a labor certificate showing workers are registered with IMSS, and a zero-deforestation certificate.

🇲🇽✊ "For us, education is the center. It is the link so that young people don't get close to criminal activity." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Plan Michoacán report, Nov 4, 2026 One year after the murder of Uruapan mayor Carlos Manzo, more than 20 federal officials reported on the social side of the Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice: 118 billion pesos planned for 2025-2030 across 12 axes, 67% advanced. Every public school student in the state now has a scholarship. Electricity reaches 99.99% of homes. In Uruapan, INEGI's survey shows about 60% less victimization, though the perception of insecurity is slower to change. The security report comes next Tuesday.
banner: PLAN MICHOACÁN: 67% DONE IN ONE YEAR

text: 🇲🇽🌎 "Regardless of the result of the election, we always seek the best relationship with the United States, always guaranteeing respect for our sovereignty, territorial integrity and collaboration without subordination." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Plan Michoacán report, Nov 4, 2026 Asked about Tuesday's US midterm elections, Sheinbaum highlighted the wins of two people of Mexican origin: the governor-elect of California and the governor-elect of Texas, each with one or both parents born in Mexico. On whether the result could unlock the USMCA review, she said Mexico negotiates with the US federal government, not Congress, and it is "very early" to know if anything changes. "The conversations continue with the secretaries and with President Trump himself."

🔥🇲🇽 "In the end, the final beneficiary was the same Casillas brothers in every case." — Raquel Buenrostro, Secretary of Anti-Corruption and Good Government, Mañanera, Nov 5, 2026 Using open sources, Buenrostro traced the network to 1983, when the Hernández Casillas brothers entered the Interior Ministry, and later CISEN. By 1999 they were electoral suppliers in the State of Mexico, where a 2005 contract scandal forced seven electoral councilors to resign. From 2014 to 2023, 23 of the 32 state electoral bodies gave their companies more than 2 billion pesos in contracts; in 2024-25, 15 bodies gave 646 million. The firms rigged bids among themselves, declared no employees, shared addresses and phones, and moved money through layers of companies, down to 96-year-olds and 18-year-olds. The Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF) has frozen the assets of 25 people and 15 companies.

🔥🇲🇽 "That's where this whole mess, this electoral mafia, comes from. It did not arise with Taddei." "Who appointed those electoral councilors? You, and all the INE councilors from 2014 to 2023." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Mañanera, Nov 5, 2026 Sheinbaum traced the companies behind the electoral-materials contracts to the Hernández Casillas brothers, who started out in the 1980s under Juan Carlos Padilla Aguilar at Renapo and then CISEN. Padilla, she said, is today a prominent member of Somos, which she called Lorenzo Córdova's party. From 2014 to 2023, the INE council led by Córdova appointed every state electoral council, and those bodies gave the brothers' companies more than 2 billion pesos in contracts. Former INE head Guadalupe Taddei must be investigated, she said, "but it was not born there."

🚨🇲🇽 "Raids against people because of their skin color and their ethnic origin." "It's sort of logical to think that something that influenced Latinos who have the right to vote in the United States to now vote for the Democratic Party would have to do with this racism." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Mañanera, Nov 5, 2026 Asked whether the Trump administration's immigration raids shaped Tuesday's US midterm results, Sheinbaum said "it's very likely." Post-election analyses show that many Latino voters, among them US citizens of Mexican origin who backed Trump in 2024, voted Democratic this time. A day earlier she had highlighted the wins of the Mexican-origin governors-elect of California and Texas.

🇲🇽⚖️ "With everything we know now, savings can very probably be made within the INE." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Mañanera, Nov 5, 2026 Under Guadalupe Taddei, the INE requested close to 47 billion pesos for 2027. The government disagreed, but by law it must send autonomous bodies' budget requests to Congress exactly as presented. It removed only the part tied to a possible 2027 public consultation, which will not take place. Sheinbaum said it is up to the Chamber of Deputies to cut the INE's budget and bring it in line with 2024, 2025 and 2026. A reporter noted Taddei had also sought an atypical increase of more than 2 billion pesos for the INE's administration directorate, 75% above 2024.

🇲🇽🎨 "The lies crash into the truth and into reality." — "Lie Detector" segment, Mañanera, Nov 5, 2026 In 2026 the well-being scholarships reach more than 19.5 million public school students. El Universal's front page attributed to UNESCO a figure suggesting the Benito Juárez scholarships discourage students. The Education Ministry (SEP) clarified it is not a UNESCO position but an academic working paper, with an estimate about a different population than the one the scholarships serve. One of its authors, Fernanda Márquez Padilla Casar, studied at a private institution from 2004 to 2010 on a Pemex scholarship. She is the daughter of María Amparo Casar, president of Mexicanos contra la Corrupción.
